name: Status quo bias
statement: An option is chosen more often when it is labelled the current one, and pre-set defaults are accepted at rates well above how often people pick the same option freely.
meaning: The claim has two halves that are usually merged. The first is a framing result. Relabel an option as the thing the decision-maker already holds, change nothing else about it, and it gets picked more often. The second is a field claim. People who have already chosen leave their choice alone, while new entrants facing the same menu choose differently. Defaults sit across both halves. A default is whatever takes effect when nobody acts, which makes it the current state by construction, so the size of default effects is routinely read as the size of the bias. That reading is disputed. A default also tells the chooser what the institution setting it recommends, and it is the one option that costs nothing to accept.

origin.note: "Status quo bias in decision making" named the effect, ran the questionnaire experiments that demonstrate it, and added field data on health-plan and retirement-fund choices. It appeared in the journal's first issue, pages 7 to 59.

evidence: The 1988 paper did two separate things. In the experiments, 486 students in economics classes at Boston University School of Management and at the Kennedy School of Government answered hypothetical decision problems in two versions. In the neutral version every option was listed without framing. In the status quo version one option was described as the position the decision-maker already occupied and the others as departures from it. Response rates fell in the same order across most cells: highest when an option sat in the status quo slot, lower when neutral, lowest when framed as the alternative to the status quo. In the four-alternative questions the ordering held in 17 of 24 cases, in the two-alternative questions 16 of 24, and in the three-alternative questions 13 of 18. The paper's own test compares the status quo rate against the non-status quo rate, and it rejects the hypothesis of no difference at the 10 percent level in 31 of 54 cases. Pooling all 66 choices, the fitted line is SQ = 0.177 + 0.830 times the neutral rate, and the matching intercept for the non-status quo position is not distinguishable from zero. Nobody was paid. The field half is a cohort comparison. Some 9,185 Harvard University employees were spread across eight health plans in 1986. Long-standing employees stayed with the incumbent Blue Cross/Blue Shield plan and new hires took the newer HMOs, and the authors calculate that transfers between plans would have to run more than ten times their actual 1986/1987 rate to bring the old cohort's distribution near the new cohort's. At TIAA, then some 850,000 participants, a 1986 survey found that 28 percent had ever changed how their premiums split between the two funds, 20 percent exactly once. Set against a twelve-year average length of participation, the authors put the annual figure at fewer than 2.5 percent. The best-known extensions are about defaults. Johnson and Goldstein put a hypothetical organ-donation question to 161 online respondents where switching cost one mouse click. Consent was 42 percent when the default was not to be a donor, 82 percent when it was to be a donor, and 79 percent with no default at all. Only the opt-in condition came out significantly lower, and opt-out did not differ from no default. Their European figures for effective consent run from 4.25 percent in Denmark to 99.98 percent in Austria, with no overlap between opt-in and opt-out countries and nearly 60 percentage points between the two groups. The same paper also regressed actual cadaveric donations on the default across countries for 1991 to 2001 and reported a 16.3 percent rise, P < 0.02, from 14.1 to 16.4 donors per million. Madrian and Shea studied one firm that switched to automatic enrolment in its 401(k) plan on 1 April 1998. The employer match, vesting, investment options and loan terms were unchanged. At 3 to 15 months of tenure, 37 percent of the cohort hired in the year before the switch participated, against 86 percent of those hired after it. Among participants hired under automatic enrolment, 76 percent contributed at the 3 percent default rate. Counting every employee in that cohort rather than the participants, 61 percent sat at the default rate in the default money-market fund and had moved neither. Recent evidence uses a different paradigm. Hamrak and Simonovits surveyed 2,016 US respondents on the legality of 13 substances, with an embedded experiment on hypothetical drugs built to match each real one's attributes. Support for the three federally legal substances ran 23.8 to 62.4 percentage points above support for their matched hypothetical versions, median 39.33, 95% CI 35.34 to 43.20. For illegal drugs the median difference ran the other way, at -12.59, 95% CI -15.44 to -9.87.

replication.headline: A preregistered replication of the naming paper found the effect in three of its four scenarios, and failed to find it in the fourth.
replication.detail: Xiao, Lam, Piara and Feldman ran two preregistered Mechanical Turk collections on four of Samuelson and Zeckhauser's scenarios, with 311 and 316 respondents completing them. Budget allocation, investment portfolios and college job offers are counted as successful and the wagon-colour scenario is not. In the first phase all four budget-allocation options were chosen more often under status quo framing than under non-status quo framing, the weakest comparison giving chi-square = 9.38, p = .002, Cohen's h = 0.44, 95% CI [0.16, 0.73]. The authors also compared status quo framing against neutral framing, which the original paper's chi-square column does not test, and three of the four options differed significantly with h from 0.38 to 0.57. Support for the investment-portfolio scenario is thinner than the summary suggests. In the second phase two of its four options differed from non-status quo framing and none differed from neutral framing. The wagon colours failed twice. In the first phase no colour differed significantly from non-status quo framing in the expected direction, and only White differed from neutral framing, chi-square = 5.06, p = .024. In the second phase two colours differed under the first comparison, one of them marginally, tan at chi-square = 3.90, p = .048 with h = 0.27, 95% CI [-0.02, 0.56]. None differed under the second comparison, and silver blue was chosen more often under non-status quo framing than under status quo framing. The authors report replication effect sizes comparable with the original for the budget and portfolio scenarios and larger for the college-jobs scenario. The default half of the literature, including the meta-analysis of 58 default studies, sits in the default effect entry, no. 180.

study.cite: Xiao, Q., Lam, C. S., Piara, M., & Feldman, G. (2021). Revisiting the status quo bias: Replication of Samuelson and Zeckhauser (1988). Meta-Psychology, 5, MP.2020.2470.

limits: The famous evidence is not experimental. Harvard's health-plan data and the TIAA allocations compare cohorts who joined at different times, and Samuelson and Zeckhauser ask in their own text whether such persistence amounts to a bias at all. Their own sequential experiment is a caution against reading persistence as bias. In the air-fleet question 79 percent and 86 percent of subjects kept their previous choice, and the marginal-probability comparison that would show a bias came out at p = .60 and p = .35. Johnson and Goldstein's country figures have the same shape: eleven countries plotted, no random assignment, and an outcome that is registration rather than transplantation. Their donation-rate estimate is a cross-country time series, not an experiment. Two later analyses find the consent gap does not carry through to donation. Arshad, Anderson and Sharif compared 35 OECD countries for 2016, 17 opt-out and 18 opt-in, and found no significant difference in deceased donors per million population, 20.3 against 15.4, but fewer living donors under opt-out, 4.8 against 15.7. A 2023 corrigendum to that paper exists, and its text could not be obtained through Kidney International, ScienceDirect, PubMed or Europe PMC, so what it revises is not known here. Güntürkün and colleagues combined panel data on 24 countries, 18 keeping opt-in throughout and six switching to opt-out between 2000 and 2023, with four further studies of which three are randomised experiments. They report that adopting opt-out raised deceased donors by 1.21 per million, 7 percent, P = 0.213, and lowered living donors by 4.59 per million, 29 percent, P = 0.026. The laboratory default literature is heterogeneous enough that a pooled figure describes a spread rather than a typical study, and the numbers behind that judgement sit in entry no. 180. No multi-site preregistered replication of the status quo framing effect was located in searches of Crossref, PubMed, Europe PMC and the Meta-Psychology archive. Xiao and colleagues remain a single laboratory running two online samples.
misreadings: The most common error is treating status quo bias, the endowment effect, no. 46, and loss aversion, no. 31, as one finding with three names. Loss aversion is a ratio fitted to risky choices, the endowment effect is a gap between selling and buying prices for a good someone holds, and status quo bias is a shift in choice caused by a label. Loss aversion is often offered as the explanation for the other two, which makes them illustrations of it rather than evidence for it. The second error is treating every default effect as a preference for the current state. McKenzie, Liersch and Finkelstein gave 88 students a choice between two one-page summaries with identical content. In the default condition 98 percent, 43 of 44, read the summary that was already on the desk; with no default, 39 percent chose it. The one default participant who chose otherwise was dropped, leaving 87 for the follow-up questions. Of the default group 30 percent agreed they had chosen it because the experimenters appeared to want them to, against none of the no-default group, and 65 percent agreed it would have been too much effort to choose the other, against 5 percent. Jachimowicz and colleagues find defaults more effective when they work through endorsement, what the choice architect seems to think the chooser should do, or through endowment. Johnson and Goldstein set out all three routes, effort, endorsement and reference dependence, and said which one dominates should change what policymakers conclude. The third error is quoting the organ-donation percentages as donation rates. They are effective consent, meaning the share who registered or who did not opt out. The fourth is treating inertia, no. 275, as another name for the bias. Samuelson and Zeckhauser use status quo inertia for participants who kept their previous choice and write that such inertia is not itself evidence of status quo bias. Some of those people may prefer that option under any conditions, so a test requires comparing the marginal probabilities.
